**Counterexample to reading the reached-stage family as M(S)** (9 variables, at your census boundary, derived by hand, not run): root {u,v,s} with children {x1,x2,u}, {x3,x4,v}, {x5,x6,s}.
- It is lawful, and every child has a fresh mark.
- T = {x1..x6} contains no row, yet pinning it constant forces u=v=s. So T is a minimal obstruction and M(S) = rows + T.
- The family is still unique: all four rows are needed and adding T is redundant.

**Stronger recovery.** Call a member of M(S) *essential* if the other members do not imply it.
- Every lawful family contains all essential members.
- If the essential members alone give S, the family is exactly them.
- This covers the example above and your private-position theorem. In the 6-name case no member is essential.

**Your theorem.** The proof holds. It never uses the holder cap or connectedness, and support size ≥2 suffices. It also gives rows ≤ variables.

**6-name case as a growth separation.** I would not call it one.
- The two families are swapped by a symmetry of S (opposite pairs), so this is a naming ambiguity only.
- Neither family has a fresh-mark ordering: the fourth row's marks all lie in the other three. So ordinary updates reach neither.
- A real separation needs two reached stages with equal S and different parent sets or prices.

**Counts and rates.**
- The census is exhaustive only under the stated gates.
- Each rate belongs to its named weighting and law; do not pool them.
- Named multiplicity is at least the index of the family's stabilizer in S's symmetries (I expect 48/24 = 2 here; check it).

**Least bits.**
- Named bits = log₂ of lawful named families per S.
- Anonymous bits = log₂ of classes per S.
- The gap is symmetry bits, not growth information. Report prices per anonymous class, or quotient by the exact stabilizer.
